question: Which statement best describes Continuous integration?
options: Continuous integration (CI) runs shared checks when code changes. It can install locked dependencies, check types, run tests, and build the site. It is like inspecting each batch before it leaves a workshop. A failing check should show which change needs attention. For example, a pull request can run type checking and tests before someone approves it. In practice, run checks on the same locked dependencies that developers use locally.

Deployment publishes a known build to a hosting environment. Connect the release to a commit or build identifier so a team can tell exactly what users received. It is like putting a batch number on a shipped product. Verify routes, assets, and runtime settings after release. For example, a release identifier lets support connect a report to the exact files deployed. In practice, record the build ID or commit hash next to release health signals.

Preview and production environments may use different settings. Secret values belong in protected hosting configuration, never in client bundles or committed files. It is like keeping a key in a locked office rather than printing it on the package. Check which variables are public before a build. For example, store an API secret in the host settings and keep it out of browser bundles. In practice, use a secret manager for credentials and expose only public configuration to the browser.

A production build turns source files into browser-ready output, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript chunks, and images. It is like packing the final product for delivery. Test that output because development mode can behave differently and hide deployment problems. For example, a production build may reveal missing environment values that a development server supplied automatically. In practice, keep preview deployments separate so a test release cannot overwrite production data.
